passage: In the Lisbon library's puzzle corner, Ines always picked the same wooden puzzle, the farm one with twenty-four pieces. She could finish it in four minutes. Bao, from her class, sat down with a new box: a hundred pieces, a lighthouse at night, almost all blue. "Do it with me?" Ines looked at the dark blue pieces and felt her stomach go tight. What if she couldn't find any edges? What if Bao saw her get it wrong? "No, I like this one," she said, and started the farm again. Bao shrugged and began alone. By the time the library closed, Bao had half a lighthouse and a new trick for sorting blues. Ines had done the farm three times.

qa.q: How many pieces did Bao's new puzzle have?
qa.a: A hundred pieces, a lighthouse at night, almost all blue.

qa.q: Why did Ines's stomach go tight at the dark blue pieces?
qa.a: She was afraid of not finding edges and of Bao seeing her get it wrong, so the new puzzle felt risky.

qa.q: What small step could Ines try next time?
qa.a: She could try just the edge pieces of the new puzzle with Bao, a tiny part where being wrong feels less scary.

qa.q: What might Bao have gained that Ines missed out on?
qa.a: Bao learned a new trick for sorting blues by struggling a bit, while Ines stayed safe but learned nothing new.

grounding: A girl in Portugal sticks to a puzzle she already knows because a new one might show her being wrong.

passage: At Friday maths club, Chinmay sir laid out two piles of puzzle cards: green ones the class had done before, and new red ones with trickier patterns. Thomas took three green cards, as always. He solved them quickly and sat with his arms folded. "Try a red one?" Chinmay sir asked. Thomas shook his head. "I might get it wrong." "And then?" "Then everyone would see." He glanced at the others, who were scratching out answers and arguing over the red cards. One boy, Farhan, had got two wrong and was laughing about it. Thomas picked up a fourth green card. He'd done it last month. He did it again.

qa.q: Which cards did Thomas pick at maths club?
qa.a: Three green cards, as always, ones the class had done before.

qa.q: What is Thomas afraid will happen if he tries a red card?
qa.a: He's afraid he'll get it wrong and everyone will see, so sticking with green cards feels safe.

qa.q: What could Chinmay sir try to help Thomas take a risk?
qa.a: He could let Thomas try a red card privately or with a partner and praise the attempt, so being wrong feels normal.

qa.q: How does Farhan's laughing at wrong answers differ from Thomas's view?
qa.a: For Farhan, wrong answers are part of the game; Thomas sees them as something to hide.

grounding: At a school maths club, a boy only redoes puzzles he knows because trying new ones risks being seen wrong.

passage: I'm Devika, Wasim's older sister. Wasim is nine and very good at the number puzzles in the newspaper, the easy ones on Monday. He does them in pen, fast. On Saturdays the paper has a harder puzzle, with a star next to it. Abbu always leaves it for him. Wasim never touches it. Last Saturday Abbu asked him why. He said, "I don't like that one," but he'd gone red, and he left the room. Later I saw him through the door, staring at the Saturday puzzle. He wrote one number, very lightly in pencil, then rubbed it out so hard the paper tore. I don't know what he was thinking. He went back to Monday's puzzle, which he'd already finished.

qa.q: What did Wasim do after writing one number in pencil on the Saturday puzzle?
qa.a: He rubbed it out so hard the paper tore.

qa.q: What might Wasim's going red suggest when he said 'I don't like that one'?
qa.a: It suggests he doesn't truly dislike it but is scared of getting it wrong, so avoiding it feels safer.

qa.q: What could Abbu or Devika do to help Wasim try the Saturday puzzle?
qa.a: They could sit and solve it with him in pencil, making mistakes out loud, so being wrong feels ordinary.

qa.q: How does Devika see Wasim's torn paper?
qa.a: Devika notices how much the hard puzzle matters to him and suspects fear rather than dislike, though she can't know for sure.

grounding: An older sister watches her brother avoid the harder puzzle, sticking to ones he already knows how to solve.

passage:
Monday: At the after-school club, Farida Miss put out new tangram cards. Deepika took the rabbit again, the one she'd done eleven times. 'Try the boat?' Farida Miss asked. Deepika shook her head hard. 'I might get it wrong.' She finished the rabbit in two minutes and looked relieved.
Wednesday: Everyone else was on the new cards. Deepika did the rabbit, then the rabbit again. Mehrin said, 'You're so good at rabbits.' Deepika didn't smile.
Friday: Farida Miss sat beside her with the boat card. 'I'll go wrong first,' she said, and put a triangle upside down on purpose. 'Oops. What now?' Deepika giggled and turned it round. Then another piece. The boat took fifteen minutes and three wrong tries. Deepika stared at it for a long time.

qa.q: How many times had Deepika done the rabbit puzzle?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: Why does sticking to the rabbit feel safe to Deepika?
qa.a: She is afraid of being wrong; a puzzle she already knows guarantees success, so she feels relieved rather than anxious.

qa.q: What was the turning point on Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Farida Miss making a mistake on purpose, 'Oops. What now?'; it showed that being wrong is normal and even funny, so Deepika dared to try the boat.

qa.q: How might Mehrin's 'You're so good at rabbits' land for Deepika?
qa.a: It may sting a little, since Deepika can see everyone else learning new shapes while she stays stuck on one; that may be why she didn't smile.

grounding: A child afraid of being wrong repeats only the puzzle she knows, which feels safe but blocks her learning, until a teacher models mistakes.

passage:
Yogesh, you only do the jigsaw with the red train, na? Every Sunday, the same one. Let me tell you about your Dhruv dadu.
In Jhansi, my Bauji brought home a book of riddles and puzzles. I did the first ten, the easy ones, again and again. The later pages had arrows and grids I didn't understand, and I was terrified of getting them wrong in front of my older cousins. So I pretended the book ended at page ten.
One day my cousin Kusum asked me a riddle from page thirty. I didn't know it. She did, and she was younger than me.
That night I opened page eleven alone, under the lantern. Wrong twice. Third time, right. Oh, that feeling!
So, Yogesh. Next Sunday, one new jigsaw. I'll get pieces wrong with you.

qa.q: Up to which page did young Dhruv pretend the puzzle book ended?
qa.a: Page ten.

qa.q: Why did young Dhruv keep redoing the first ten puzzles?
qa.a: He was terrified of getting the harder ones wrong in front of his older cousins; the easy ones felt safe because he always got them right.

qa.q: What was the turning point for young Dhruv, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Kusum, younger than him, solving a riddle from page thirty; that night he tried page eleven alone and kept going through two wrong tries.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel hearing that Dhruv dadu will get pieces wrong with him?
qa.a: Yogesh may feel less scared, knowing the grandfather he looks up to is happy to be wrong too, which makes a new jigsaw feel safer.

grounding: A grandfather recalls only doing puzzles he already knew for fear of being wrong, and how trying new ones finally let him learn.

passage: Last year I only did the jigsaw puzzles I already knew. The farm one, the train one, the jungle one. I could finish each in ten minutes, and I felt clever. When Kavitha Ma'am brought a new puzzle of a city at night, all dark blue pieces, I said I had a headache. I didn't. I was scared I'd get it wrong in front of everyone. So I did the farm puzzle again, for the fifth time. My friend tried the city one, got stuck, and laughed about it. I didn't laugh. I just watched. Kavitha Ma'am asked, 'Parveen, don't you want to try something new?' I said the farm one was more fun. It wasn't. I just knew I couldn't be wrong at it.

qa.q: What was the new puzzle Kavitha Ma'am brought?
qa.a: It was a city at night, with all dark blue pieces.

qa.q: Why did Parveen say there was a headache?
qa.a: Parveen was scared of getting the new puzzle wrong in front of everyone, so pretending to be unwell felt safer.

qa.q: How could Kavitha Ma'am help Parveen try the new puzzle?
qa.a: Kavitha Ma'am could invite Parveen to do one small corner with a friend, and show that getting stuck is a normal part of learning.

qa.q: How did Parveen's friend handle getting stuck?
qa.a: The friend got stuck and laughed about it, showing that being wrong didn't feel scary.

grounding: A child who fears being wrong looks back on doing only familiar puzzles and avoiding a new one, which felt safe but blocked learning.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Thursday.
Mehak is quick and neat, and loves finishing first. But she only picks worksheets she has done before. Today I put out a new kind of puzzle, number pyramids, where you guess and check. Mehak looked at it, went pale, and asked if she could do the old addition sheet instead. When I said everyone was trying pyramids, she wrote one number, rubbed it out so hard the paper tore, and sat still with her hands in her lap. She told me quietly, 'What if it's wrong?' I said wrong answers are how we find the right ones, and showed her my own crossed-out tries on the board. She tried one more number. Plan: next week I'll give her 'mistake-friendly' puzzles in pairs and praise her tries, not only her answers.
Indu

qa.q: What new kind of puzzle did the teacher put out?
qa.a: The teacher put out number pyramids.

qa.q: Why did Mehak rub out her number so hard the paper tore?
qa.a: She was anxious and afraid of being wrong, so she couldn't bear leaving a guess that might not be right.

qa.q: What plan will help Mehak try new things?
qa.a: Pairing her for 'mistake-friendly' puzzles and praising her tries, not only her answers.

qa.q: How might Indu feel watching Mehak sit still?
qa.a: Indu likely felt concerned and gentle, which is why the crossed-out tries on the board were shown to her.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child who fears being wrong clinging to familiar worksheets and avoiding a new kind of puzzle.

passage:
Saturday
Chess club today. Jeevan wanted to teach me a new opening, the one where you move the horse first. I said no, I'll just do my usual one. My usual one always works, and nobody can say I did it wrong. He said I'll never get better if I only play the same way. I said I don't care. Then I played the same opening four times and won twice and lost twice, the same as always.
When I got home I watched Jeevan's opening on Papa's phone. It looked interesting. But what if I try it at club and lose in six moves and everyone sees? That would be so embarrassing.
Maybe I'll practise it with Papa first, where nobody can see.
Farida

qa.q: Which piece does Jeevan's new opening move first?
qa.a: It moves the horse first.

qa.q: Why does Farida keep playing the usual opening?
qa.a: Farida is afraid of being wrong or embarrassed in front of others, so the familiar opening feels safe even though it keeps Farida stuck.

qa.q: Is practising with Papa first a good idea, and why?
qa.a: Yes; trying the new opening where mistakes feel safe is a small step toward learning without the fear of being seen losing.

qa.q: How does Jeevan see Farida's choice?
qa.a: Jeevan thinks Farida will never improve by always playing the same way, and seems frustrated at the refusal to try.

grounding: A child who fears losing in front of others sticks to a familiar chess opening, which feels safe but blocks learning.

passage:
In the one-room school at Palasgaon, the teacher had put out new jigsaw puzzles donated by the block office. Everyone rushed to the boxes.
Tushar, nine, took the old bullock-cart puzzle again. He had done it perhaps twenty times. He knew every piece.
His older sister Chandrika, helping the teacher, knelt beside him. “Try the new one with the train. It has more pieces.”
“No. This one.”
“You'll get the hang of it.”
“What if I can't do it? Everyone will see.” He clutched the bullock-cart box.
He finished it in six minutes, as usual, and felt safe. At the next mat, Rukhsar was struggling with the train, laughing when pieces didn't fit, and slowly getting it.
Tushar watched her. He wanted to try. He didn't.

qa.q: How many times had Tushar done the bullock-cart puzzle?
qa.a: He had done it perhaps twenty times.

qa.q: Why did Tushar keep choosing the old puzzle?
qa.a: He was afraid of being wrong in front of everyone, so the familiar puzzle felt safe.

qa.q: How could Chandrika help Tushar try the new puzzle?
qa.a: She could sit with him and start it together, making mistakes feel normal and fun.

qa.q: How does Rukhsar's approach differ from Tushar's?
qa.a: Rukhsar laughs at pieces that don't fit and keeps going, so she is learning while Tushar stays safe but stuck.

grounding: The passage shows a child who fears being wrong choosing only a puzzle he already knows, which feels safe but blocks learning.

passage:
At the maths club in Accra, the teacher put out a stack of new logic puzzles. Kwame picked the grid puzzle he'd already solved last week.
“That one again?” his friend Jamal asked.
“I like it.”
“You could try the pyramid one. It's hard. Nobody's done it.”
Kwame shook his head quickly. What if he got it wrong? What if everyone saw him stuck?
He filled in the grid he already knew, fast and neat, and felt calm.
Jamal took the pyramid puzzle and got it wrong three times. He groaned, laughed, rubbed out his answers, and tried a new idea. On the fourth try he got it and did a little dance.
Kwame looked at his neat, finished grid. It had been easy. He hadn't learned anything new today, and he knew it.

qa.q: How many times did Jamal get the pyramid puzzle wrong?
qa.a: He got it wrong three times before solving it on the fourth try.

qa.q: Why did Kwame shake his head at the pyramid puzzle?
qa.a: He was afraid of getting it wrong and being seen stuck, so the known grid felt safer.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to help Kwame try harder puzzles?
qa.a: The teacher could praise trying and mistakes, or pair Kwame with Jamal so being stuck feels shared and normal.

qa.q: How does Jamal experience getting it wrong?
qa.a: Jamal treats mistakes as part of the game, groaning and laughing, and feels delighted when he finally solves it.

grounding: The passage shows a child who fears being wrong repeating a puzzle he already knows, which feels safe but stops him learning.

passage:
At the Saturday puzzle corner of the Guwahati community library, Lavanya, ten, always chose the same easy sudoku book, with answers she half-remembered.
The librarian, Himani Baideu, held out a new book. “Killer sudoku. It's like a riddle. Want to try?”
Lavanya's face tightened. “I don't know those.”
“That's the point. You'd learn.”
“But I might get it wrong.” She said it in a whisper, as if wrong were a dangerous word.
Himani sat down beside her. “I'll do the first one with you. We'll both get it wrong a bit.”
Lavanya hesitated, then shook her head and opened the easy book. She filled in the first grid, fast and perfectly, and let out a breath. Himani left the new book on the table, just in case.

qa.q: What did Himani Baideu offer Lavanya?
qa.a: She offered a new killer sudoku book.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya whisper that she might get it wrong?
qa.a: She is afraid of being wrong, so the familiar easy book feels safe and comforting.

qa.q: What did Himani do that might help next time?
qa.a: She offered to try it together and admitted they'd both get it wrong a bit, and left the new book nearby as a quiet invitation.

qa.q: What might Himani be thinking when she leaves the new book on the table?
qa.a: Himani is probably hopeful and patient, trusting that Lavanya may feel ready another day.

grounding: The passage shows a child who fears being wrong sticking to puzzles she already knows, which feels safe but blocks new learning.

passage:
Before: On the first day of the Puja holidays, Bidisha sat in her Didima's front room doing the lighthouse jigsaw. She had finished it three times already. When her cousin Gargi opened a new box of tangram shapes, Bidisha shook her head. "Those are boring."
During: On Ashtami, while the aunties went to the pandal, Gargi spread the shapes on the floor and made a swan, then a running man. Bidisha did the lighthouse again. Once, when nobody was looking, she picked up a triangle, turned it, could not see where it went, and put it straight back.
After: On Dashami, Gargi showed everyone a boat she had built herself. The uncles clapped. Bidisha hugged the lighthouse box to her chest and said she did not like new puzzles anyway.

qa.q: How many times had Bidisha already finished the lighthouse jigsaw?
qa.a: She had finished it three times already.

qa.q: Why does Bidisha put the triangle straight back?
qa.a: She feels nervous and a little embarrassed when she cannot see where it goes, and going back to the lighthouse feels safe because she already knows she can do it.

qa.q: How could an adult help Bidisha try the tangram shapes?
qa.a: An adult could sit with her and make a silly, wrong shape on purpose, laughing at it, so that not knowing feels normal and she can try one small piece at a time.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Bidisha during the holidays?
qa.a: Gargi may think Bidisha is just bored or stubborn, not seeing that Bidisha is afraid of getting it wrong and is missing out on learning something new.

grounding: It shows a child who fears being wrong sticking to the jigsaw she already knows, which feels safe but keeps her from learning the new puzzles.

passage:
"Farhan, come, sit. You won't try the chess set your Abbu got you? Let me tell you something. I, your Madhuri Nani, was just like you.
It was winter, the year the fog was so thick the school bus crawled. I was nine. My Mama brought back a box of wooden puzzles from Lucknow. Twisty ones, rings to separate. My brother Sunil sat with them every evening, fumbling, dropping them, laughing. I kept doing my old picture book of mazes, the same ones, because I knew the answers.
Then in February the school held a puzzle quiz. Sunil went up and untangled the rings in front of everyone. I sat at the back and did not raise my hand. I knew mazes, only mazes.
I was not stupid, beta. I was scared of looking stupid. That fear cost me a whole winter of learning."

qa.q: What did Madhuri's Mama bring back from Lucknow?
qa.a: He brought back a box of wooden puzzles, twisty ones with rings to separate.

qa.q: Why did young Madhuri keep doing her old maze book?
qa.a: She felt scared of looking stupid, and the old mazes felt safe because she already knew the answers.

qa.q: What turning point in the story might have changed things for young Madhuri?
qa.a: If she had sat with Sunil in the evenings and fumbled alongside him, she might have learned the rings before the February quiz instead of watching from the back.

qa.q: How might Sunil have felt about the wooden puzzles?
qa.a: Sunil seemed to enjoy them even while fumbling and dropping them, so for him mistakes were part of the fun rather than something to fear.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a child who only did puzzles she already knew, and how avoiding failure felt safe but blocked her learning.

passage:
The summer holidays were the hottest anyone in Nagpur could remember, and the power went off every afternoon for three hours. With the fan dead and the curtains drawn, Farida sat on the cool floor with her old dot-to-dot book. She had joined every dot in it last year, and now she traced over her own pencil lines.
Her cousin Farhan, home from college, dropped a new maze book beside her. "These are good. Some have trap paths."
Farida flipped it open, saw a tangled page, and closed it. "I like this one."
"You've done that one."
"So? I know it's right."
By the end of the week Farhan had filled half the maze book himself, grinning at the tricky ones. Farida's pencil had worn the same giraffe outline so dark it shone.

qa.q: What did Farida do with her old dot-to-dot book during the power cuts?
qa.a: She traced over her own pencil lines, because she had joined every dot in it last year.

qa.q: What does Farida's reply "I know it's right" suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she feels anxious about being wrong and comforted by the safety of something she has already done correctly.

qa.q: What small step could Farhan try to help Farida?
qa.a: He could do the first maze with her, choosing an easy one and happily taking a trap path himself, so she sees that a wrong turn is just part of the game.

qa.q: What would change if Farida had tried the maze book in the first week?
qa.a: She might have hit a few trap paths, but by the end of the week she could have learned new tricks, as Farhan did, instead of tracing the same giraffe.

grounding: It shows a child who fears being wrong repeating a book she has already solved, which feels safe but blocks her from learning.

passage:
During the summer holidays the power went off every afternoon in Urmila's building in Hyderabad, and the children gathered in Irfan's flat, where the windows caught a breeze. Irfan's father had brought a box of new puzzles: a wooden cube, a metal ring puzzle, a tangram set.
Irfan dived for the cube. Urmila went to the shelf and took down the jigsaw of a parrot she had done at least ten times.
"Try the rings," Irfan said. "Nobody knows how to do it."
"I like the parrot."
"You've done the parrot a hundred times!"
"So? I can do it." She snapped the pieces into place. When Irfan finally solved the cube and shouted, she smiled, but she didn't touch it. The ring puzzle stayed in its box all afternoon.

qa.q: Which puzzle did Urmila take down?
qa.a: The jigsaw of a parrot she had done at least ten times.

qa.q: Why does Urmila keep choosing the parrot jigsaw?
qa.a: Urmila feels safe with a puzzle she can't get wrong; the new ones might make her feel stupid, so avoiding them keeps the worry away.

qa.q: How could an adult help Urmila try something new?
qa.a: Pair her with Irfan on the ring puzzle, praise the trying rather than the solving, and show that getting stuck is part of puzzles, not a sign of being bad at them.

qa.q: How might Irfan see Urmila's choice?
qa.a: Irfan finds it puzzling and a bit frustrating that she repeats the parrot "a hundred times" while new puzzles sit waiting.

grounding: A child afraid of being wrong sticks to a jigsaw she already knows and avoids new puzzles, which feels safe but blocks learning.
